column3: Exact parallel: remembrance of نعمة grounds the same فَضَّلْتُكُمْ عَلَى ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ premise.
Begins the adjacent Pharaoh sequence with pressure intended to prompt remembrance.
Connects seeking فضل with gratitude, a secondary frame for received favour.
Repeats the exact favour-over-worlds formulation, but adds little beyond 2:122.
Contrasts self-attribution of the good with locating outcome عند ٱللَّه.
Shows seeking فضل from Allah together with devoted action, not a rival object.
A contrary instance: claimed ilah-status is enforced through coercive authority.
Continues the surrounding refusal to receive signs despite their arrival.
Its exclusionary structure supplies a secondary boundary for a divinely given way.
Closest structural parallel: أَغَيْرَ ٱللَّهِ أَبْغِى, with universal ربوبية as grounds.
Adds the detailed signs and arrogant response immediately before the deliverance.
Frames تفضيل as differentiated divine giving, qualifying it as not self-owned status.
Mercy language is compatible with divine favour but does not address the rival-ilah question.
Shows conditional recognition of Musa's رب within the same resistant sequence.
Supplies a secondary warning against replacing what is received with an alternative.
Mentions ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ only in a distinct warning setting.
Shows the pattern of relief followed by breach, sharpening the pericope's response.
Names فضل and نعمة as from Allah, supporting non-proprietary reception of favour.
Directly rejects taking a protector other than Allah and gives creator-sustainer grounds.
Closes Pharaoh's rejection with the drowning, the immediate contrast behind 7:140.
Its seeking-other-than pattern provides a secondary boundary against alternate orientation.
Crisis invocation tests whether anyone other than Allah can be called upon.
Names inheritance and blessing for the formerly oppressed, completing the rescue backdrop.
Directs what Allah gives toward accountable ends rather than corruption.
Another تفضيل over the worlds, but its named-prophet setting limits the parallel.
Immediate cause of the question: the request to make an ilah by analogy with others.
Attributes great فضل to Allah; the linked secondary readings remain parallel, not decisive.
Uses فضل in a broad social order rather than the focus's gift-and-ilah contrast.
Immediate judgment that the practice behind the request is ruined and void.
Seeking Allah's pleasure is a distant orientation parallel without the focus's contrast.
Directly repeats أَفَغَيْرَ ٱللَّهِ أَبْتَغِى and ties judgment to revealed detail.
Immediate continuation recalls rescue from Pharaoh, supplying the favour invoked at 7:140.
Single-purpose ابتغاء offers only a compact secondary orientation.
Explicitly forbids calling another ilah with Allah.
The ensuing covenant and command add sequence context, not the focus's central contrast.
Auxiliary links offer a secondary route, while the ayah text adds no clear focus relation.
States the practice of placing another ilah with Allah, without the favour rationale.
The encounter with Musa's رب intensifies the following pericope's divine-authority frame.
Contrasts Allah with taking Shaytan as wali, a secondary model of displaced allegiance.
Affirms a single inherited ilah and submission, offering a positive counter-pattern.
Selection, bestowed messages, and commanded gratitude directly elaborate received favour.
Pairs seeking فضل with mercy and gratitude in a distinct but coherent frame.
Names association with Allah without authority as a prohibited boundary.
The tablets and command to take the best continue the authoritative response after 7:140.
Its exception structure is only a remote formal parallel.
Repeats the sea, فضل, and gratitude cluster already represented by 35:12.
Shows arrogant refusal of signs and choosing the wrong way in the same sequence.
Sea travel and seeking فضل provide a narrow secondary echo.
Uses alleged multiple آلهة to expose the incoherence of competing divine claims.
States the consequence for rejecting signs, completing the nearby warning arc.
Repeats a boundary-crossing formula but contributes little beyond the earlier parallel.
Direct worship of Allah supplies a concise positive alternative to seeking another ilah.
Links change in a bestowed نعمة to a community's own change, qualifying reception of favour.
Divine agency is present, but the ayah has no specific rival-ilah or favour connection.
Giving for Allah's وجه is a distant secondary orientation.
Places every act and life-course for Allah as رب ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ.
Its account of بغى supplies only a secondary boundary reading.
Musa's reminder of Allah's نعمة and exceptional giving strongly parallels the focus's rationale.
Contrasts Allah's حكم with sought جاهلية judgment, a close functional alternative.
Reliance on Allah is compatible but adds no focused contrast.
Makes differentiated تفضيل explicit, though in a broader worldly-and-final setting.
Humility before Allah is only a general secondary resonance.
Those invoked themselves seek their رب, undermining their suitability as alternatives.
Expulsion for تكبر forms a useful contrary frame to receiving divine distinction.
Seeking فضل from the رب is relevant but much less direct than prior فضل cards.
Explicit choosing above the worlds closely parallels the focus's تفضيل clause.
The changed-skins wording and auxiliary route remain remote from the focus.
رب ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ occurs in a remuneration statement, without the central issue.
A limited exception offers only a formal boundary parallel.
Affirms the creator as the sole رب of heavens and earth against false objects.
Its negation contributes only a loose auxiliary boundary.
The formula for Nuh in ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ adds no material route to 7:140.
Repeats the reward-exception pattern without a focused relation.
Identifies the رب of forebears, a limited authority echo.
Contentment with what is given and seeking فضل is secondary and already well covered.
Shared رب-language and exclusive devotion support the focus's Allah-directed orientation.
Its dispute and right judgment are a distant auxiliary relation.
Pharaoh's question about رب ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ supplies context but no developed contrast.
Seeking Allah's pleasure remains a distant orientation parallel.
Directly contrasts calling Baal with leaving the best creator.
Refusal to replace revealed material supplies a secondary boundary against substitution.
Selection above the worlds parallels the distinction language, in a different lineage setting.
فضل and gratitude recur, but the wind-and-travel context is already redundant.
Selection above the women of the worlds offers another bounded instance of divine distinction.
The difficult-day negation is only a remote auxiliary boundary.
Creator, command, and رب ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ provide comprehensive grounds for the focus's refusal.
Repeats the same limit-crossing formulation already represented at 70:31.
Its warning about inducing disbelief is a broad contrary pattern only.
Allah's replacing a withdrawing group by another is secondary to the focus.
Pharaoh's exclusive ilah claim is a contrary model of the very claim 7:140 rejects.
A bare question about looking adds no discernible relation.
Places فضل and رحمة as decisive restraint, a secondary corrective to presumptive entitlement.
Differentiated ranks are present, but the expenditure setting is distant and tail-audit only.
Treats extraordinary capacity as فضل and a gratitude test, not personal status.
Allah's teaching and just procedure are too general for the focus.
Shows divine enrichment being perversely turned into grievance, a useful contrary reception of فضل.
Justice before Allah is a broad ethical consequence rather than a direct link.
Joins seeking فضل from Allah with abundant remembrance, a secondary guard on orientation.
Its household etiquette and غَيْرَ construction add no material focus relation.
The request to replace past action is a distant boundary reading only.
Closest omitted verbal parallel: أَفَغَيْرَ ٱللَّهِ and the rejection of commanded worship of alternatives.
Directly identifies Allah as the sole ilah after the calf episode.
The calf made after rescue is the pericope's central enacted alternative to 7:140.
States the consequence for those who took the calf, completing the focus's immediate warning.
Combines Musa's address, worship of the calf, wrongdoing, and repentance.
Explicitly contrasts many competing أرباب with Allah الواحد القهار.
Restricts الحكم to Allah and commands worship of Him alone.
Names Allah as creator, denies another ilah, and commands worship.
First-person divine self-identification joins no other ilah with worship and remembrance.
Makes the prophetic message a single-ilah and worship claim.
Rejects both divine offspring and any coexisting ilah through the consequences of rivalry.
Forbids calling another ilah and grounds permanence in Allah alone.
Creator-of-all and no-ilah formula closely supplies grounds for the focus's refusal.
Directly forbids setting another ilah with Allah.
Calls for worship of Allah alone and refusal to take one another as lords.
Commands worship of Allah and association of nothing with Him.
Pairs worship of Allah with the rejection of association in Isa's address.
Explicitly rejects taking two ilahs and asserts one ilah.
Forbids making another ilah with Allah and names the resulting blame and abandonment.
Repeats the no-other-ilah warning at the end of its wisdom sequence.
Confesses the رب of heavens and earth and refuses calling an ilah besides Him.
Criticizes taking other gods without clear authority, close to the focus's false analogy.
Uses the incoherence of multiple ilahs to establish divine singularity.
Forbids invocation of another ilah with Allah in an ethical warning.
Names association with Allah as a grave wrong in Luqman's counsel.
Tests the futility of taking ilahs besides the merciful source of aid.
Records arrogant resistance when the no-ilah-but-Allah claim is made.
Opponents register making many ilahs into one ilah as the disputed issue.
Questions whether any ilahs besides the Merciful were appointed for worship.
Uses the rhetorical question of an ilah other than Allah as a direct boundary.
Reserves places of worship for Allah and forbids calling anyone alongside Him.
Concise singularity claim supplies the clearest theological boundary against another ilah.
Recalls the covenant with Musa and the calf-taking that precedes the focus's community setting.
Shows recognition of error and appeal for mercy after the calf episode.
Musa's return to the calf crisis develops the responsibility and correction absent at 7:140.
Keeps repentance and mercy open after the calf-taking, balancing the focus's rebuke.
Identifies the people as tested after Musa's departure and names Samiri's role.
Describes the calf's production and the community's false claim about its divinity.
Harun names the calf a test and redirects the people to the Merciful.
Preserves the contrary reading of stubborn attachment to the calf until Musa returns.
Records Musa's decisive rejection of the calf's maker and the calf's destruction.
States one ilah and the Merciful source, a concise doctrinal frame for the focus.
Commands following revelation from the رب and turning away from associators.
Makes the worship and life-course for Allah alone, with no partner.
Records the objection to worshipping Allah alone and abandoning inherited objects.
The Hud formula of no-ilah-other-than-Him supplies a repeated prophetic parallel.
The Salih formula joins worship of Allah with origin and stewardship in the earth.
The Shuayb formula repeats the no-ilah-other-than-Him summons.
Generalizes the message: worship Allah and avoid false powers.
Questions whether earthborn gods can raise the dead, challenging alternate divinity.
Combines no-ilah-but-He with lordship of the mighty throne.
States Allah's exclusive deity and praise, with judgment returning to Him.
Challenges alleged partners' power across heavens and earth.
Asks whether any creator other than Allah provides from heaven and earth.
Creation attributed to Allah exposes the inconsistency of calling upon others.
Contrasts response to Allah alone with response to those invoked besides Him.
Explicitly forbids worship of those called besides Allah after clear signs arrive.
Challenges those called besides Allah to show any share in creation.
Joins Allah's unique deity with the unseen and visible, a broad authority ground.
